subject: اللغة الإنجليزية
lesson: Grammar Recall: present perfect and present perfect continuous; verb forms
outcomes: Know when to use the present perfect and the present perfect continuous
Use 'for' with a length of time and 'since' with a starting point
Use both tenses to talk about congestion and everyday situations

tf.s: The present perfect continuous is formed with have/has been + verb-ing.
tf.why: For example: I have been waiting.

tf.s: 'I've been waiting for an hour' shows an action that is still continuing.
tf.why: The waiting started in the past and is still going on.

tf.s: 'I've lost my phone' focuses on how long the action lasted.
tf.why: It focuses on the result now: the phone is lost.

tf.s: We use 'for' with a period of time, like 'for half an hour'.
We use 'since' with a period of time, like 'since two hours'.
tf.why: 'Since' needs a starting point: since 3 o'clock.

tf.s: 'Where have you been?' is an example of the present perfect.
Car ownership rose by 10% between 2013 and 2014 in the text.
The text says there were more than 10,000 cars in 1970.
tf.why: The text says there were fewer than 1000 cars in 1970.

tf.s: 'Traffic has been flooding the city centre for months' shows a situation that started in the past and continues now.
tf.why: The present perfect continuous shows ongoing actions.

tf.s: 'I haven't been to Dubai for 2011' is correct.
tf.why: 2011 is a starting point, so use 'since 2011'.

boxes.q: I was stuck in traffic ___ half an hour.
boxes.why: Half an hour is a length of time.
3 o'clock is when the waiting began.

boxes.q: Traffic ___ the city centre for months.
boxes.why: The action started in the past and continues.

boxes.q: Which word goes with a length of time?
Which sentence shows a result now?
boxes.why: The focus is on the result: no phone now.

boxes.q: By how much did car ownership rise (2013–2014)?
Why do some drivers speed in the text?
boxes.why: They are late because of traffic.

boxes.q: How many cars were there in 1970?
boxes.why: The text says fewer than 1000 cars.

hunt.q: Place of the college in the text

mcq.q: How do we form the present perfect continuous?
mcq.why: For example: She has been working.

mcq.q: What is the difference between 'for' and 'since'?
Which example from the cartoon is in the present perfect?
What does the text say drivers do to make up time?
mcq.why: Late drivers speed, which is dangerous.

mcq.q: Your friend arrives very late. What do you say to show you have waited a long time?
o: I've been waiting for you for over an hour!
I will wait for you tomorrow.
I waited you since an hour.
mcq.why: The present perfect continuous stresses the long, continuing action.

mcq.q: Someone asks: 'Have you packed yet?' Which reply uses the present perfect continuous?
mcq.why: have been + packing shows an action continuing up to now.

o: Miss Smith has been getting up earlier for weeks.
Miss Smith has been getting up earlier since weeks.
Miss Smith have been get up earlier for weeks.
Miss Smith is got up earlier since weeks.
mcq.why: has been + -ing, and 'for' + a length of time.

mcq.q: Why is 'has been growing' used for the number of cars?
o: The growth began in the past and is still continuing
mcq.why: The present perfect continuous shows an ongoing process.

mcq.q: Compare 'I've been waiting for an hour' and 'I've lost my phone'. What is the main difference?
o: The first shows duration; the second shows a result
mcq.why: Continuous focuses on how long; simple focuses on the result.

mcq.q: Fewer than 1000 cars in 1970 and a 10% rise from 2013 to 2014. What do these facts show?
o: The number of cars has been growing, causing more congestion
mcq.why: More cars on the roads means more congestion.
